module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Factorial primes

A factorial prime is a prime that is one more or one less than a factorial. It
is conjectured that there are infinitely many factorial primes.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Factorial prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factorial_prime)
- [OEIS A088054](https://oeis.org/A088054)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace FactorialPrime

/-- A factorial prime is a prime one above or one below a factorial. -/
def IsFactorialPrime (p : ℕ) : Prop :=
  p.Prime ∧ ∃ n : ℕ, p = n.factorial + 1 ∨ n.factorial = p + 1

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem seven_isFactorialPrime : IsFactorialPrime 7 := by
  refine ⟨by norm_num, 3, Or.inl ?_⟩
  norm_num

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem twentyThree_isFactorialPrime : IsFactorialPrime 23 := by
  refine ⟨by norm_num, 4, Or.inr ?_⟩
  norm_num

/-- There are infinitely many factorial primes. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem infinitely_many_factorial_primes :
    Set.Infinite {p : ℕ | IsFactorialPrime p} := by
  sorry

end FactorialPrime

sources_consulted: OEIS A088054, complete entry via the official data mirror: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oeis/oeisdata/main/seq/A088/A088054.seq
review.notes: Checked all four declarations. The definition faithfully captures primes of the form n! ± 1, both example theorems match the source, and the infinitude statement matches Wikipedia’s conjecture. The research-open status remains consistent with the sources. Scratch checks in /workspace/review/scratch.lean compiled successfully, proving that n.factorial = p + 1 is equivalent to p = n.factorial - 1 and that restricting indices to positive naturals changes nothing. Boundary tests exclude 0 and 1 and produce exactly 2, 3, 5, 7, 23 below 32. Both existing example proofs are sorry-free. OEIS’s main page was access-blocked; its full entry was read through its official data mirror, with sequence values checked against the accessible b-file.
